crocodylus-lucivenator:study:1.title: Lucy’s peril: A Pliocene crocodile from the Hadar Formation, north-eastern Ethiopia (Journal of Systematic Palaeontology, 2026)

facts.statement: Crocodylus lucivenator was described by Brochu and colleagues.
facts.quote: Authors: Brochu et al.

facts.statement: Crocodylus lucivenator lived during the Pliocene epoch.
facts.quote: Age: Pliocene

facts.statement: The type locality for Crocodylus lucivenator is the Hadar Formation.
facts.quote: Type locality: Hadar Formation

facts.statement: Fossils of Crocodylus lucivenator have been found in Ethiopia.
facts.quote: Country: Ethiopia

facts.statement: Crocodylus lucivenator belongs to the genus Crocodylus.
facts.quote: genus: Crocodylus

facts.statement: The specific epithet of this extinct crocodile is lucivenator.
facts.quote: species: lucivenator

facts.statement: The species was formally named in 2026 by Brochu and colleagues.
facts.quote: authority: Brochu et al., 2026

facts.statement: Crocodylus lucivenator is an extinct crocodile from the Late Pliocene Hadar Formation in Ethiopia.
facts.quote: Crocodylus lucivenator is an extinct species of crocodile from the Late Pliocene Hadar Formation of Ethiopia.

facts.statement: Crocodylus lucivenator appears to be closely related to Paleoafrican Crocodylus species from East Africa rather than modern African crocodiles.
facts.quote: appears to be closely related to paleoafrican Crocodylus species from East Africa rather than the crocodiles that inhabit the continent today.

facts.statement: The holotype of Crocodylus lucivenator is specimen A.L. 138-16, a complete cranium with a matching lower jaw.
facts.quote: The holotype of Crocodylus lucivenator is specimen A.L. 138-16, a complete cranium with the matching lower jaw and the most complete specimen known.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen comes from the SH-1 submember of the Sidi Hakoma Member.
facts.quote: The holotype specifically comes from the SH-1 submember of the Sidi Hakoma Member

facts.statement: Brochu and colleagues referred numerous other fossil remains to the species, spanning from the Kada Hadar Member down to the Denen Dora Member.
facts.quote: Brochu and colleagues also referred an enormous number of other fossil remains to the species spanning all the way to the Kada Hadar Member and covering the intermediate Denen Dora Member as well.

facts.statement: The species name lucivenator derives from Latin words meaning "light" and "hunter".
facts.quote: The species name "lucivenator" derives from the Latin words "luci" and "venator" meaning "light" and "hunter" respectively.

facts.statement: The name alludes to Lucy, a famous specimen of Australopithecus afarensis found in the Hadar Formation.
facts.quote: The first part of the name also has a second meaning, as it simultaneously alludes to Lucy, a famous specimen of the early hominid Australopithecus afarensis also known from the Hadar Formation.

facts.statement: A significant feature of Crocodylus lucivenator is a rostral boss, an expanded skull structure stretching along the dorsal surface just before the eyes.
facts.quote: A significant feature of Crocodylus lucivenator is the presence of a so-called rostral boss, an expanded structure of the skull that stretches along the dorsal surface of the skull just before the eyes.

facts.statement: The second posterior knob on the maxilla is described as more pronounced than the midrostral boss.
facts.quote: Importantly, the second, more posterior knob is described as actually being more pronounced than the midrostral boss.

facts.statement: The skull table of Crocodylus lucivenator is trapezoidal and primarily formed by the frontal, parietal, postorbital, and squamosal bones.
facts.quote: The skull table is trapezoidal in shape and formed mostly by the main body of the frontal, the parietal bone, the postorbitals and the squamosals.

facts.statement: The postorbital bones form pronounced squamosal horns that are most developed in the largest specimens.
facts.quote: The moderately upturned dorsal surface of each postorbital is briefly interrupted by a notch near the contact with the squamosals, which continue on to form a pair pronounced squamosal horns, which are most pronounced in the largest specimens.

facts.statement: The parietal bone contacts the frontal and squamosals broadly but has only a short contact with the postorbitals.
facts.quote: The parietal broadly contacts both the frontal and squamosals, but only has a short contact with the postorbitals along the outer edges of the supratemporal fenestrae.

facts.statement: The lateral skull table groove, infratemporal fenestra, and postorbital bar are located on the side of the skull.
facts.quote: On the side of the skull lie the lateral skull table groove, the infratemporal fenestra and the postorbital bar, which separates the infratemporal fenestra from the eyesockets.

facts.statement: The incisive foramen is circular with a posterior notch and two deep pits for the first dentary teeth.
facts.quote: The incisive foramen is described as circular with a modest notch in its posterior margin and there are two deep pits for the reception of the first dentary teeth anterolateral to this opening.

facts.statement: The contact between the premaxillae and maxillae on the palatal surface forms a distinct W-shape.
facts.quote: On the palatal surface the contact between the premaxillae and maxillae forms a distinct W-shape.

facts.statement: The fourth premaxillary teeth and the fifth and tenth maxillary teeth were the largest in the upper jaw.
facts.quote: The largest premaxillary teeth was the fourth while the largest maxillary teeth were the fifth and tenth.

facts.statement: The teeth of Crocodylus lucivenator display a classic interlocking pattern.
facts.quote: The teeth of Crocodylus lucivenator display the classic interlocking pattern expected of the group.

facts.statement: The first dentary tooth slid into a deep notch in the premaxilla and may have broken through the dorsal surface with age, exposing the tip even when jaws were closed.
facts.quote: The first dentary tooth would have slid into a deep notch present in the palatal surface of the premaxilla and some specimens show that with age the tooth may have even broken through the dorsal surface, leaving the tip exposed even when the jaws were shut.

facts.statement: Isolated osteoderms from the Hadar Formation attributed to Crocodylus lucivenator vary in shape based on their body position.
facts.quote: Several isolated osteoderms from the Hadar Formation have also been attributed to Crocodylus lucivenator and vary in overall shape, likely in accordance with their position on the body.

facts.statement: Some osteoderms were circular or D-shaped and likely formed part of the nuchal shield or covered the flanks.
facts.quote: Several are circular or D-shaped and likely were part of the nuchal shield atop the neck or covered the flanks.

facts.statement: Wider-than-long osteoderms likely formed the main dorsal armor covering the back.
facts.quote: Others are wider than long and were likely part of the main dorsal armor covering the back.

facts.statement: Osteoderm surfaces were covered in pits with a single crest, though one specimen had a uniquely curved crest.
facts.quote: The surface of the osteoderms was covered in pits and featured a single crest, though one particular specimen is unique from the other Hadar Formation material in having a much more curved rather than straight crest.

facts.statement: The largest specimens of Crocodylus lucivenator reached lengths of 4 to 5 meters and weights of 300 to 600 kilograms.
facts.quote: The largest specimens of Crocodylus lucivenator reached a length between 4-5 m and likely reached a weight between 300-600 kg.

facts.statement: Crocodylus lucivenator belongs to the Palaeoafrican Crocodylus clade, which is distantly related to modern Neoafrican crocodiles like the Nile and Sacred crocodiles.
facts.quote: The resulting trees were largely in agreement with prior studies that recovered a distinct monophyletic clade of Crocodylus species commonly referred to as Palaeoafrican Crocodylus that is only distantly related to the crocodiles that inhabit Africa today, referred to as the Neoafrican Crocodylus, composed of the extant Nile and Sacred crocodile.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Crocodylus lucivenator in a basal position within the genus, branching off before the Indopacific clade and the split between Neoafrican and Neotropic taxa.
facts.quote: The strict consensus recovered the Palaeoafrican clade and by extension Crocodylus lucivenator in a basal position relative to extant members of the genus, having branched off before the Indopacific clade as well as the split between Neoafrican Crocodylus and the clade formed by Neotropic taxa and Crocodylus checchiai proper.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the Palaeoafrican group including Crocodylus lucivenator should clade with modern Neotropic Crocodylus, as alternative phylogenetic results are possible.
facts.quote: Brochu and colleagues note some differences with other phylogenetic analyses of crocodylids. Some alternative results are also possible, as it would only take one additional step for the Palaeoafrican group to clade with modern Neotropic Crocodylus due to the shared presence of a rostral boss.

facts.statement: A specimen of Crocodylus lucivenator preserves five furrows and a puncture wound on its lower jaw.
facts.quote: Specimen A.L. 126-11 of Crocodylus lucivenator preserves several lesions along the dentary including five furrows and a putative puncture wound

facts.statement: Healing bone texture suggests the crocodile survived the injury and lived for a significant time after the encounter.
facts.quote: the texture within and surrounding these injuries is described as irregular and spongy, suggesting that the animal not only survived the encounter but that bone had already undergone significant healing by the time the animal died

facts.statement: Evidence indicates the wounds were caused by another crocodile rather than a mammal.
facts.quote: This combination of traits excludes the possibility that the wound was inflicted by a mammals and instead suggests that the animal was injured by another crocodile

facts.statement: The injury patterns suggest the crocodile used feeding maneuvers like the death roll or head thrashing during an attack.
facts.quote: Such a pattern is typical for animals that utilize inertia when feeding, which in the case of crocodiles include maneuvers such as the death roll, thrashing of the head and the quick release and seizure of prey with the jaws

facts.statement: Due to its niche and size, the primary threat to individual Crocodylus lucivenator was likely other members of its own species.
facts.quote: Given their nische and size, it was likely that the biggest threat to individual Crocodylus lucivenator were other members of the same species

facts.statement: Crocodylus lucivenator is interpreted as a large generalist ambush predator and likely the apex predator of its environment.
facts.quote: Given the size and robust skull-build, Crocodylus lucivenator is interpreted to have been a macro-generalist ambush predator, likely the apex of its native environment

facts.statement: The Hadar Formation environment consisted of mixed woodlands and grasslands with large paleolakes at certain times.
facts.quote: The Hadar Formation is described as preserving a mixed environment of woodlands and grasslands with large palaeolakes present during some points in time

facts.statement: Crocodylus lucivenator fossils are found in three of the four members of the Hadar Formation: Sidi Hakoma, Denen Dora, and Kada Hadar.
facts.quote: Crocodylus lucivenator was present throughout three of the formations four members, the Sidi Hakoma, Denen Dora and Kada Hadar Members

facts.statement: The oldest member of the Hadar Formation was wetter and more wooded, while younger members were deposited under drier conditions.
facts.quote: Among these the oldest, the Sidi Hakoma Member, was the wettest and most heavily wooded, while the younger members were deposited under increasingly drier conditions

facts.statement: The Hadar Formation contains fossils of Australopithecus afarensis, which likely fell prey to Crocodylus lucivenator.
facts.quote: The formation also preserves the fossil remains of the early hominine Australopithecus afarensis, which would have likely fallen prey to the crocodiles

facts.quote: PBDB name: Crocodylus (genus), Laurenti 1768

facts.quote: Family: Crocodylidae

facts.statement: The genus Crocodylus belongs to the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The genus Crocodylus existed from the Campanian to the Holocene, spanning 83.6 to 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Holocene (83.6 to 0 million years ago)

facts.statement: A study titled 'Lucy's peril' describes a Pliocene crocodile from the Hadar Formation in north-eastern Ethiopia.
facts.quote: Study title: Lucy’s peril: A Pliocene crocodile from the Hadar Formation, north-eastern Ethiopia

facts.quote: Authors: Christopher A. Brochu, Stephanie K. Drumheller, Christopher Campisano, Getahun Tekle, Tomas Getachew, Jason J. Head, Nathan C. Platt, Daniel Leaphart
